records.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
records.author: ziofill
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.

So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.

I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!

It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.

A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there

I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

records.title: Show HN: Fleetlayer – Framework for running many AI agents on multiple machines
records.author: nathan_f77
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I ran into many problems when I started running lots of Claude Code sessions in parallel. I quickly ran out of usage, so I signed up for more Claude subs (which Anthropic terms allow.)

Running so many different accounts meant that I couldn't use claude.ai artifacts anymore, because the browser has to be signed in to the same account in order to access them. It's a pain to keep signing in and out of accounts. This also broke the Claude in Chrome extension because that can also only be signed into a single account.

Then I needed to manage AI agents that run on my laptop, a VM on my laptop, and multiple VMs on my home server. Claude Code has a messaging feature which is very useful, but agents can't see each other when they run on different machines. The Claude in Chrome extension only works for agents running on the same machine, so my remote agents couldn't help me with anything in the browser. It's really handy when they can access services that I'm already signed into.

I set out to solve all of these problems and I ended up building Fleetlayer. It's a control plane and a node binary that you run on all your machines and VMs to connect them all together. It connects to Herdr (and other session managers soon), and it makes it possible for all your AI agents to message each other and access tools and resources on other machines (with permission.)

It has a lot more features too: routing webhooks to agents, single sign-on, access rules, approvals, audit logs, remote terminals, remote browser sharing, centralized AI account sign-ins, session summaries, secrets management, and pages and apps (our own self-hosted version of claude.ai artifacts).

A few ways to think of it:

- The "Nextcloud" of claude.ai features (your own self-hosted artifacts, remote control, browser use, etc.)

- The "Arch Linux" of OpenClaw (build your own agentic systems from swappable components and plugins)

You can run everything on your laptop to try it out, then easily move any component to a different machine. If you want to build a proper production-grade home server to run many AI agents, Rust builds, and CI runners, I've also open sourced my own setup as a boilerplate IaC example repo. You just need to install Proxmox and then point your AI agent at the guide [1].

I'd be interested to know if anyone else would find Fleetlayer useful. Please let me know if you have any feature requests!

[1] https://fleetlayer.ai/docs/guides/server-setup/

records.title: Show HN: Baxel – a collective gallery of 8×8 pixel sprites
records.author: achtaitaipai
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I made Baxel, a small gallery of 8×8 sprites. You draw one in the browser with ten colours plus transparent, publish it, and it gets its own address and joins a feed anyone can browse. You can draw and publish as a guest, no account needed.

What I like about it is people adding to one shared collection. It's a bit like art without an artist: each drawing is tiny and takes a minute, and what ends up being interesting is the wall of them, not who made which. Most of the rules follow from that.

- Publishing puts a sprite under CC0, for good. It belongs to the collection once it's in. Drafts stay yours until you publish.

- No two published sprites can hold the same drawing.

- A whole sprite is 64 characters, one per pixel. That string is what the database stores, what the page turns into a PNG for download, and what the server draws the link-preview image from.

Stack is tRPC on Hono, Drizzle, React with TanStack Router, and a dependency-free PNG encoder for the previews. Happy to answer questions.

records.title: Show HN: Flowmaps – the logic layer for agents and developers
records.author: micahke
records.storyText:
Hi everyone,

I've spent the last few months building a tool called Flowmaps. It's the logic layer for agents and developers. It sits between your team and your codebase and constantly builds and maintains a logical map of what the code does.

Agents are already writing a large volume of code. The bottleneck has become the process of understanding what it does. Agents don't make the same mistakes that programmers do; instead the errors are usually related to logic that the agent doesn't have full context on.

Flowmaps helps you understand the what the code does without having to read it line-by-line. For developers, this means reviewing and understanding agent PRs without losing touch with the code. Agents also share an understanding of the code in a way that ensures consistency and less token spend across the organization.

I'm looking for some early users to try it out for free and provide some feedback. If you're interested, add yourself to the waitlist or send an email to demo@flowmaps.ai.

Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: SoundEtch, an open source podcast/media editor for the desktop browser
records.author: bfbsoundetch
records.storyText:
I've been working on this project for a few years, and thinking about it for a few more years. Ever since the pandemic when I did my entire job on a little Chromebook with browser-based tools; why not make an Audacity for the browser?

Well, it turned out there were already a few "Audacities for the Browser" like https://audiomass.co/ (posted here a couple times already), https://naomiaro.com/waveform-playlist/, and a literal Audacity compiled to WebAssembly https://wavacity.com/. SoundEtch is kind of a beefed up version of those.

I made it with podcasters and other spoken-word creators in mind, rather than musicians, since there are a number of browser DAWs already e.g. OpenDAW.

Everything is streamed to and from disk (OPFS), with an optional cloud backup. You can close or crash the browser tab, even in the middle of recording, and your data is still there when you open it back up. This also means you can load huge files; my parents' desktop with 8gb RAM handled this 5 hour stereo mp3 I found on archive https://archive.org/details/2023-09-08/2023-09-10.mp3.

There's a transcription-based editing tool like you get with Riverside and Descript. Mine uses IBM's Granite Turbo model, plus some Codex/Claude tweaking to get word-level timestamps. The result is, to my knowledge, much faster and more accurate than any other browser/local ASR out there. It has a few quirks, though, like only emitting lower-case letters and spaces.

I also added a WebRTC meeting room with up to 4 guests. It doesn't have a TURN service, so some networks will block you from connecting.

Since AI coding assistants are so good these days, I was able to add video support pretty easily. You can import, export, and record video, add that transcript with the current word highlighted, etc.

The editing is pretty basic for now: you can trim the clips, move them around, add some effects including noise removal from DeepFilterNet (https://github.com/Rikorose/DeepFilterNet).

I appreciate your taking a look and any feedback you have! The code is at https://github.com/bfbsoundetch/SoundEtch

records.title: Show HN: GPT Plays Civilization
records.author: Routine8502
records.storyText:
Hey HN,

I've always been a big fan of the Civ games, and was always frustrated at how terrible the AI was. So I got curious about whether LLMs could play Civ well, or not! I thought about having the agents interact with the GUI directly, but something about that seemed like the wrong approach. For one thing, it seemed to me like images would cost way more in tokens. For another, LLMs seem like a different kind of intelligence from humans, so why would an interface meant for humans be optimal for them?

Anyway, I spend a few weeks modifying Unciv [0], an open-source reimplementation of Civ V to have the right endpoints and views for an agent to be able to play civ in the same way a person could. You can see the first game running at the link. So far, it looks like the GPT models are able to play a reasonable game - definitely better than the built-in AI, which was my barometer for success! You can find the harness here: https://github.com/varchasgopalaswamy/unciv-ai. Let me know what you folks think!

[0]: https://github.com/yairm210/Unciv

records.title: Show HN: Quark – native apps with react. no webview or Chromium
records.author: sinisterMage
records.storyText:
Hi HN! i got Excalidraw running on the desktop without a webview or source changes to upstream using strange quark, (note that collaboration was off for my testing) i built it because it should be easy to build native desktop apps that are cross platform without learning a whole new stack, or 3 for that matter if you are using the native toolchains for each platform

for each platform Strange Quark keeps the parts of a browser that React apps depend on and replaces the rest with native code: 1. Your app and react-dom run unmodified in V8. 2. react-dom talks to squark-dom, a DOM written in JavaScript. React and libraries see ordinary DOM nodes, events and CSSOM objects. 3. Every DOM change becomes a 16-byte record in a journal. The journal streams into a Rust copy of the document. 4. Stylo(the CSS engine Servo and Firefox share) styles that document. Taffy and Parley lay it out. 5. A GPU renderer draws it through wgpu and Vello, on its own thread. i would love to hear technical feedback and criticism!

records.title: Show HN: Guess a London bus route or a World River from its shape on the map
records.author: laechoppe
records.storyText:
I like geography and geo quizzes in all shapes and forms. I also moved to London and became a big fan of the TfL identity (not the reliability). So I made a daily game: one London bus route is drawn on the map with its number hidden, and you get three guesses. Wrong guesses are drawn on the map too, so you can see how far off you were. Then I realised London buses are too niche, and I wanted a game with a lower entry bar, so I made one with rivers of the world.

The routes come from TfL Open Data. All 657 of them are in, so any route you type can be drawn. The first time I saw a route as an almost straight line I was sure it was a bug. It wasn't, it was just a route going along a straight street. Hello, 32!

With rivers, I didn't think until the very last moment that the base map labels them, so the map was giving the answer away. Now every water label is removed. The web version has 80 major world rivers from OpenStreetMap, and the iPhone app adds packs for the UK and India.

It's plain HTML and JS modules with no build step, MapLibre with OpenFreeMap tiles, hosted on Netlify. There are no accounts or tracking; your streak is kept in your browser's localStorage. It's free on the web and plays the same daily puzzle as the iPhone apps.

Any feedback is welcome - how to expand it, what to add, which cities, which other games - anything.

records.author: juliusgeo
records.storyText: A few days ago I was joking with coworkers that it would make signing contracts significantly more fun if they were on scrolls with wax seals. scrollusign.com was $11 to purchase, so I made it. It's hosted on Cloudflare--the backend is a Rust worker with D1 as the DB. The scroll is rendered using GLSL shaders with LYGIA for PBR effects. As with most stupid jokes, it is significantly funnier the more effort is put into it, so the wax pools realistically and the quicker you click "sign" the more of an indentation it makes on the cooling wax. Anyone with a link can sign a scroll. Please don't use this for actual binding contracts.

records.title: Show HN: Using Claude and Codex to beat the original Netflix Prize challenge
records.author: quan
records.storyText:
I had a lot of fun working on the Netflix Prize 20 years ago but didn't come anywhere close. For the past two months, I got Claude and Codex working on it together.

I initially thought surely with all the advancement in AI, this would be solved within a week with my $20 ChatGPT plan. It turned out to be more difficult and my Codex kept getting rate limited. I had to upgrade to max and eventually added Claude to the mix.

Progress was slow for a whole month until a Claude session didn't follow the repo guidelines for promoting scores by mistake. It ended up improving by training much harder on a model that would've been rejected much earlier. It turned out the guideline was too strict and short sighted. The coding agents were abandoning sound strategies too early, some results to worse before they got better. You can kinda spot this happening around Nov 16 on the plot https://mquan.github.io/netflix_challenge/#timeline

The 10% improvement was finally achieved yesterday and I'm so happy and relieved that I can now downgrade my plans :). If you're curious, the final breakthru came from combining temporal SVD++ with item-item neighborhood models. At least that's how AI explained its solution in one sentence. I did learn a few new tricks steering agents on topics I'm not a domain expert and built tools to help them collaborate.

Project repo: https://github.com/mquan/netflix_challenge

records.title: Show HN: Renovate-preview – dry-run Renovate locally, see updates as a table
records.author: kwentine
records.storyText:
I maintain several Renovate configs as part of my work, and commonly experience friction when I have to debug or adjust them: it usually involves typing rather cumbersome podman commands to perform dry runs, and examining lines of JSON logs.

renovate-preview aims to ease that process: `renovate-preview path/to/repo` runs Renovate's local platform in a container, and prints the dependencies it found and the updates it would propose.

`renovate-preview @owner/repo --config renovate.json` applies a local config to a remote repository, which shows the PR titles and branches. Output as a table, JSON, or a self-contained HTML page.

It's a single Python package with no dependencies (`uv tool install renovate-preview`), and it never pulls images or writes to repositories.

Similar and complementary tools I know of: renovate-pretty-log facilitates examining debug logs, and the Renovate Config Debugger simulates configs in the browser.

I'd love feedback and hope that it may prove useful to some!

records.title: Show HN: Sync MacroFactor CSV to Obsidian for a Local Food Base Usable with AI
records.author: switchupcb
records.storyText:
I synchronized my MacroFactor CSV exports into a local-first, spreadsheet-free nutrition and food-asset database inside Obsidian (works on Desktop/iOS/Android and uses zero external APIs).

The open-sourced template scripts help you make food decisions with recursive ingredient management and food queries which support 56-nutrients (macronutrients, vitamins, minerals, and amino acids).

Here are technical details. - Food ID: Every food gets a Base36 hash ID (`food_<b36>`). - Same Name, Diff Macro resolution: The sync engine lets you resolve these conflicts in an Obsidian Base using frontmatter properties (`set_as_final_version`, `set_as_unique`, `duplicate_of`) without overriding user-defined notes or properties. - Recursive ingredient management: Foods contain an `[[Ingredient]]` property and any `banned` ingredient propagates on sync. Unbanning an ingredient also restores the ban state of an item before a propagated ban.

The core MacroFactor food log and brand history synchronization template is MIT-licensed in the repository. The README also links to an optional pre-configured 40+ file Starter Vault with the Base UIs, a diet planner, double-entry ledger, and route generator (Dijkstra + TSP: for routes optimized by cost, time, kcal, etc).

What other health, nutrition, or personal logs have you synced into a Markdown note system to use as structured context with AI and what problems are you solving with it?

records.title: Show HN: Turbotap – Open-Source CLI for AI Agents to Drive an iPhone over Wi-Fi
records.author: MaxTeabag
records.storyText:
I’ve been trying to make more of my daily life AI-driven, and my iPhone was becoming the bottleneck. If an app didn’t have a web version, an MCP, or an API, I still had to pick up the phone and do it myself.

After lots of searching I finally found a solution that worked. I put a spare iPhone in developer mode, installed WebDriverAgent, and left it on my home Wi-Fi. WebDriverAgent is built on Apple’s official UI testing framework. It’s literally computer use for iPhone.

I tried mirroring the screen with AirPlay and even streaming a camera, but nothing beat WebDriverAgent. Stock WebDriverAgent was still slow in a lot of apps, so I patched it and had an agent keep improving it by trying it across tons of apps. That became Turbotap.

Now I can just ask AI to change a setting, stress-test my app on a real iPhone, or do something in an app I used to have to do by hand. Honestly, I built it out of irritation and increasing inflammation in my hands, but it’s unlocked so many things I can automate with LLMs. The AI can use the actual iPhone app the same way I would, even if there’s no web version, MCP, or API. That’s why I’m excited to share it.

You need Xcode on a Mac to sign and install WebDriverAgent over USB. Once it’s running, you can drive the phone headlessly from a Mac or Linux machine on the same Wi-Fi.

It’s free and open source. https://github.com/Maxteabag/turbotap

records.title: Show HN: Sonic Pi as a VST3/AU plugin – live coding inside your DAW
records.author: samaaron
records.storyText:
I squeezed all of Sonic Pi - including SuperCollider's scsynth - into a dynamic lib that runs inside your DAW's process. VST3 on macOS and Windows, AU on macOS.

It follows the host's tempo and transport, takes MIDI and audio in, sends MIDI out, and runs as multiple instances. Randomisation is deterministic, so bouncing the same project twice gives the same audio.

This has all been possible thanks to SuperSonic - my port of SuperCollider's scsynth. The challenge was re-architecting a multi-process multi-language app that included Erlang, Ruby, C++, to a single library that runs directly inside the DAW's process, with the audio rendered directly in the host's callback.

The examples on the page run the same engine compiled to WASM, so you can hear exactly what you'd get without installing anything.

The Sonic Pi app and web versions remain free and the hope is that sales from this plugin will help fund further open source work.

records.title: Show HN: I gave my AI Agents Production backed Memory
records.author: SubomiG
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m building Codela to help coding agents learn from what happens after their code ships. I realized that my AI agent writes a change, the tests pass, and it gets deployed. Then in production a problem happens, I fix it, but what it did wrong and why never reaches the agent, so futures session usually make the same mistake.

So I built Codela which checks every deploy against how my app actually behaves in production (via my monitoring tool signoz) , learns from the ones that broke it, and teaches my agents so they don’t repeat the mistake.

Would love any feedback on this, thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Pasteup – Paste screenshots into file upload fields
records.author: JohnGorp
records.storyText:
I'm currently a CS student, so that means a lot of file uploads to my university's janky website. I hated having to sort through the file picker just to attach an assignment open the next tab over. Pasteup is a Chrome extension that lets you press Cmd+V / Ctrl+V on the page instead, it finds the corresponding file box and attaches them automatically (if there are multiple it opens a picker).

Moreover I added an automatic file converter, so for things like CSV, txt, and code, it automatically converts it to the right format. This means my workflow went from going to the assignment sorting through 15 finder folders and uploading to ctrl a ctrl c ctrl v.

The file converter is pretty smart, and supports a lot of formats. If the field only takes PDF or JPG, it converts the file before uploading. It also turns copied spreadsheet cells into a CSV, JSON into a .json, and Figma's "Copy as SVG" into an image.

If you're already in any text boxes or editors it does nothing. If the site handles paste itself (FilePond, chat apps), it goes first, and Pasteup does nothing.

It runs entirely locally: no servers, no analytics, no network requests, no third-party libraries.

I'd love to hear about sites where it picks the wrong field or gets in the way or just any feedback in general!
